choices.text: A 1,2-dihaloalkane, with the halogens on adjacent carbons
An alkane with both halogens on the same carbon
choices.why: Vicinal means the halogens are on neighboring carbons: a 1,2-dihaloalkane.

choices.text: An alkene with a halogen on a double-bond carbon
choices.why: That is a vinylic halide, the intermediate in the twofold elimination.

choices.text: A 1,3-dihaloalkane, with one carbon between the halogens
choices.why: In a vicinal dihalide the halogens sit on adjacent carbons, as in a 1,2-dihaloalkane.

explanation: A vicinal dihalide is a 1,2-dihaloalkane: the two halogens are on adjacent carbons. Treating one with an excess of strong base removes HX twice and gives an alkyne.

prompt: Which reagent converts a vicinal dihalide into an alkyne?

choices.text: An excess of a strong base such as KOH or NaNH2
An excess of Br2 or Cl2
choices.why: Halogens add to alkenes to make vicinal dihalides. They don't remove HX.

choices.text: An excess of HBr in acetic acid
choices.why: HBr adds to multiple bonds. Making an alkyne requires removing HX, which takes a strong base.

choices.text: An excess of aqueous acid such as H2SO4
choices.why: Acid doesn't remove HX. The section uses an excess of strong base to eliminate HX twice.

explanation: Treating a 1,2-dihaloalkane with an excess of a strong base such as KOH or NaNH2 causes a twofold elimination of HX and gives an alkyne. The full mechanism is deferred to Chapter 11.

prompt: How many molecules of HX are eliminated when one molecule of a vicinal dihalide is converted into an alkyne?
explanation: The reaction is a twofold elimination of HX. The first elimination gives a vinylic halide, and the second gives the alkyne, so two HX are removed in all.

prompt: Which sequence converts trans-1,2-diphenylethylene, C6H5CH=CHC6H5, into diphenylacetylene, C6H5C≡CC6H5?

choices.why: The order is reversed. The base has no HX to remove until Br2 has made the dihalide, and Br2 added last would just leave a dibromide.
HBr adds only one halogen. Eliminating HBr from that alkyl bromide just gives back an alkene.
Water is not a strong base. A strong base such as KOH is needed to eliminate HBr twice.

explanation: Adding Br2 to the alkene gives the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane. KOH in ethanol then eliminates two HBr to give diphenylacetylene in 85% yield. This halogenation/dehydrohalogenation sequence takes an alkene to an alkyne.

prompt: When trans-1,2-diphenylethylene is converted into diphenylacetylene, what compound forms in the first step, the addition of Br2?

choices.why: Br2 adds one bromine to each carbon of the double bond, giving a vicinal (1,2) dihalide.
That is the final product. It forms only after base removes two HBr.
This vinylic bromide forms during the base step, after the first HBr is eliminated. Adding Br2 gives a dibromide.

explanation: Br2 adds across the C=C bond to give the vicinal dibromide 1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane. KOH in ethanol then removes two HBr, by way of a vinylic bromide, to give diphenylacetylene.

prompt: In the section's example, what is the percent yield of diphenylacetylene from 1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane and KOH in ethanol?
explanation: The twofold elimination of HBr with KOH in ethanol gives diphenylacetylene in 85% yield, along with water and KBr.

prompt: Through what kind of intermediate does the twofold dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide pass?

choices.text: A vinylic halide, with the halogen on a double-bond carbon
An alkane with no halogen left
choices.why: An alkane has no multiple bond. After the first elimination the molecule is an alkene that still carries one halogen.
The number of halogens goes down at each step. After one HX is lost, only one halogen remains, on a double-bond carbon.

choices.text: An alkyl halide with one halogen and no double bond
choices.why: The first elimination forms a double bond, so the intermediate is an alkene with a halogen, not a saturated alkyl halide.

explanation: The first elimination of HX turns the vicinal dihalide into a vinylic halide: a halogen attached to a double-bond carbon. The second elimination turns that into the alkyne. That is why vinylic halides themselves also give alkynes when treated with strong base.

prompt: HOCH2CH=C(Cl)CH3, (Z)-3-chloro-2-buten-1-ol, is treated with 2 equivalents of NaNH2 and then H3O+. What product forms?

choices.why: The base doesn't replace Cl with H. It removes HCl, which turns the double bond into a triple bond.
The triple bond forms between the two carbons that were doubly bonded, C2 and C3, not at the end of the chain.
The –OH group is not removed. Only HCl is eliminated, so the product keeps its CH2OH group.

explanation: A vinylic halide is the intermediate in the twofold elimination, so a vinylic halide on its own gives an alkyne with strong base. Eliminating HCl from HOCH2CH=C(Cl)CH3 makes a triple bond between the former double-bond carbons, giving 2-butyn-1-ol, HOCH2C≡CCH3.

prompt: Which compound gives 2-butyne, CH3C≡CCH3, when treated with an excess of NaNH2?

choices.why: With only one halogen, just one HX can be eliminated, and that gives an alkene, not an alkyne.
The bromines are on C1 and C4, not on adjacent carbons. A twofold elimination to an alkyne needs a vicinal (1,2) dihalide.
This alkene has no halogen to eliminate. It would first have to add Br2 to give the vicinal dihalide.

explanation: 2,3-Dibromobutane is a vicinal dihalide, with bromines on C2 and C3. Excess strong base eliminates two HBr from it, leaving a triple bond between C2 and C3: 2-butyne.

prompt: Which starting compound gives 3-hexyne, CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH3, when treated with Br2 and then an excess of strong base?

choices.why: The triple bond forms where the double bond was, so 1-hexene would give 1-hexyne.
The triple bond forms where the double bond was, so 2-hexene would give 2-hexyne.
An alkane has no double bond for Br2 to add to, so no vicinal dihalide forms.

explanation: Br2 adds to 3-hexene to give the vicinal dihalide 3,4-dibromohexane. Twofold elimination of HBr then leaves a triple bond between C3 and C4, where the double bond was: 3-hexyne. This halogenation/dehydrohalogenation sequence is the section's route from an alkene to an alkyne.
